summary:
NABD is an interactive dashboard that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations to map how wildfires changed vegetation in Laânoussar–Sefrou, Morocco, Gironde, France, and Ávila–Burgohondo, Spain. Users can compare before-and-after radar images, move through satellite passes, and click a point to see and hear how its radar signal changed over time.

In Sefrou, NABD estimated a 473-hectare fire perimeter, compared with a reported 480 hectares. NASA’s optical OPERA product also detected vegetation loss in 77.6% of the radar-detected scar where optical observations were available. These comparisons help users see where the evidence agrees and where further checks are needed. NABD addresses Dancing with the SARs by turning satellite measurements into an explorable record of wildfire damage that can help guide follow-up surveys.
details:
Wildfire impacts can be difficult to map when clouds or smoke obscure optical imagery. NABD uses L-band NISAR radar to examine vegetation change across three 2026 fires. The project is designed for land managers, researchers, and communities exploring where to prioritize post-fire surveys.

Our Python pipeline crops and aligns NISAR Level 2 GCOV scenes, filters radar speckle, and compares median cross-polarized backscatter (HV) before and after each fire on the same satellite track. Nearby unburned areas provide a reference for differences between passes. The pipeline maps connected areas of vegetation loss near the fire and groups them by the magnitude of the radar signal drop. These classes describe radar-based severity. The analysis uses NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, and Rasterio.

The web dashboard uses JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js, Three.js, and the Web Audio API. Users can drag a before-and-after divider, inspect individual locations, and listen to a radar time series as musical notes. The optical comparison layer shows where Landsat and Sentinel-2 observations in NASA’s OPERA DIST-ALERT product also indicate vegetation loss.

In Laânoussar–Sefrou, NABD estimated a 473-hectare perimeter, compared with a reported 480 hectares. The estimated perimeters were 38,643 hectares in Gironde and 30,995 hectares in the Ávila–Burgohondo analysis window. The Ávila scar reaches the edge of that window. Terrain, moisture, and gaps between acquisitions affect the estimates. The timeline dates mark when changes were observed by the satellite, and later changes in signal provide a starting point for investigating vegetation recovery.

Codex and Claude Code assisted with project development. The wildfire maps and reported metrics were derived from satellite observations and the project’s processing pipeline.
